At both ends of the body are adjustable bridges, often of ivory or hardwood. A crossbar or sliding device changes the sounding length, mostly of elm or oak. A few fine instruments use precious woods such as rosewood or ebony for the body. Modern versions may use steel or nylon strings.
單弦樂器為古代音樂與科學實驗器具，見於蘇美文字，有人認為畢達哥拉斯於公元前六世紀: The monochord is an instrument of ancient music and scientific experiment, found in Sumerian writing, and some hold that Pythagoras reinvented it in the sixth century BC. In the Middle Ages it served as a teaching aid for the mathematical relations of intervals, and around the year 1000 Guido of Arezzo is credited with the invention of the movable bridge. In 1618 Robert Fludd designed his monochordum mundi, linking the intervals to the Ptolemaic cosmos, and in 1637 Mersenne used it to study string length and tension. In the nineteenth century Denmark developed the psalmodikon, which replaces the movable bridge with a fretted fingerboard; it spread to Scandinavia and America and was later revived by folk musicians. Microtonal and just-intonation composers too have built multi-string variants with movable bridges.

Its range is limited to a single string, and the pitch can change continuously by changing the length, giving a smooth glide. Because the construction is simple and there is no elaborate resonating body, the sound is direct rather than rich, its resonance relatively primitive and its volume small. Its timbre sits between a string instrument and percussion; beside the warmth of a guitar or a zither the monochord is leaner and more transparent, and beside the musical bow, though the principle is the same, the different body gives a different density of sound. On the whole its sound is pure and has a sense of history, well suited to showing the most basic resonance of a string.

The monochord is a chordophone of antiquity that served both music and scientific experiment, its historical culture area being Europe / Greece. Its basic construction is one string fixed at both ends, stretched over a resonator or a long board, with a movable bridge, a fixed bridge and scale marks. It is played by plucking, or by changing the length of the string to give different pitches, to demonstrate the mathematical relations between intervals, frequencies and ratios. In the Hornbostel–Sachs classification it is 314.122, traditionally a board zither. In the Middle Ages it was mostly a teaching tool; today it appears in multi-string variants and in third-bridge techniques in microtonal, just-intonation and experimental music.
